title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
subject: Physics
subtitle: Class 12 HSC & MHT-CET • Rapid Revision Deck

cards.q: What is the Photoelectric Effect and who discovered it?
cards.a:
The phenomenon of instantaneous emission of electrons (photoelectrons) from a metallic surface when exposed to electromagnetic radiation of sufficiently high frequency (above threshold frequency ν₀).
Discovered by Heinrich Hertz (1887); investigated in detail by Hallwachs, Lenard; explained by Albert Einstein (1905).
cards.hint: Electrons are emitted only when light frequency ν ≥ ν₀.

cards.q: Define Threshold Frequency ν₀, Threshold Wavelength λ₀, and Work Function Φ₀.
cards.a:
Threshold Frequency ν₀: Minimum frequency of incident light required to liberate photoelectrons.
Threshold Wavelength λ₀: Maximum wavelength of incident light for emission (λ₀ = c / ν₀).
Work Function Φ₀: Minimum energy required to knock an electron out of metal surface: Φ₀ = h ν₀ = h c / λ₀ (SI unit: Joule or eV).
cards.hint: Cesium (Cs) has the lowest work function (~2.14 eV) among metals, making it highly sensitive to visible light.

cards.q: Define Stopping Potential (Cut-off Potential) V₀.
cards.a: The minimum retarding (negative) potential applied to the collector plate with respect to the emitter at which the photoelectric current drops to EXACTLY ZERO: e V₀ = K_max = (1/2) m v_max².
cards.hint: Stopping potential measures the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons directly in electron-volts (eV).

cards.q: State Einstein's Photoelectric Equation in its standard forms.
cards.a:
h ν = Φ₀ + K_max = h ν₀ + (1/2) m v_max² = h ν₀ + e V₀.
In terms of wavelength: h c / λ = h c / λ₀ + e V₀.
cards.hint: Based on Planck's quantum theory: one single photon is absorbed by one single electron in an all-or-nothing interaction.

cards.q: Four Fundamental Laws of Photoelectric Emission?
cards.a:
1. Rate of photoelectron emission (saturation current) is directly proportional to INTENSITY of incident light.
2. Maximum kinetic energy K_max (and stopping potential V₀) depends linearly on FREQUENCY ν, independent of intensity.
3. Below threshold frequency ν₀, NO emission occurs, no matter how intense the light is.
4. Emission is INSTANTANEOUS (time delay < 10⁻⁹ s).
cards.hint: Wave theory failed because it predicted emission should depend on intensity and predicted a significant time delay.

cards.q: Graph of Stopping Potential V₀ vs Frequency ν of incident light: Slope and Intercepts?
cards.a:
Equation: V₀ = (h / e) ν - (Φ₀ / e).
Slope of line = h / e (UNIVERSAL CONSTANT, identical for all metals!).
x-intercept (frequency axis) = Threshold frequency ν₀.
y-intercept (potential axis) = - Φ₀ / e.
cards.hint: Top MHT-CET favorite! Graph is a straight line whose slope is always h/e regardless of the target metal.

cards.q: Properties of a Photon: Energy, Momentum, Velocity, and Rest Mass?
cards.a:
Energy: E = h ν = h c / λ.
Momentum: p = E / c = h / λ.
Speed: c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum (independent of frame of reference).
Rest Mass: m₀ = 0 (a photon cannot exist at rest; it always travels at speed c).
cards.hint: Photons are electrically neutral and are NOT deflected by electric or magnetic fields.

cards.q: What is Radiation Pressure P and Force F exerted by a completely absorbing vs completely reflecting surface?
cards.a:
Absorbing surface: Force F = P_rad / c = I A / c | Radiation pressure P = I / c.
Reflecting surface: Force F = 2 P_rad / c = 2 I A / c | Radiation pressure P = 2 I / c, where I is intensity of radiation.
cards.hint: A completely reflecting mirror experiences TWICE the force and radiation pressure of an absorbing black surface.

cards.q: State the de Broglie Hypothesis of Matter Waves.
cards.a:
Moving particles of matter (electrons, protons, atoms) exhibit wave-like properties under suitable conditions.
de Broglie Wavelength: λ = h / p = h / (m v), where h is Planck's constant (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s) and p is linear momentum.
cards.hint: Matter waves are NOT electromagnetic; they are probability waves associated with the position of moving particles.

cards.q: Formula for de Broglie wavelength λ of an electron accelerated through potential difference V?
cards.a: λ = h / √(2 m e V) = 1.228 / √V nm = 12.28 / √V Å (Angstroms).
cards.hint: Super high-yield 10-second shortcut! For V = 100 Volts: λ = 12.28 / √100 = 12.28 / 10 = 1.228 Å.

cards.q: de Broglie wavelength of a gas molecule/neutron of mass m at absolute temperature T?
cards.a:
Average kinetic energy: K = (3/2) k_B T ⇒ p = √(2 m K) = √(3 m k_B T).
λ = h / √(3 m k_B T).
cards.hint: Shows that thermal neutrons at room temperature have de Broglie wavelength comparable to atomic lattice spacings (~1 Å).

cards.q: de Broglie wavelength of an alpha particle and proton accelerated through same potential V?
cards.a:
λ = h / √(2 m q V).
Since m_α = 4 m_p and q_α = 2 q_p: m_α q_α = 8 m_p q_p.
Ratio: λ_p / λ_α = √[ (m_α q_α) / (m_p q_p) ] = √8 = 2 √2 ≈ 2.83.
cards.hint: Proton has ~2.83 times larger de Broglie wavelength than alpha particle for same accelerating voltage V.

cards.q: Davisson and Germer Experiment: Purpose and key observation?
cards.a:
Purpose: Direct experimental confirmation of de Broglie's matter wave hypothesis for electrons.
Observation: Fine beam of 54 V electrons scattered by a Nickel crystal showed a sharp diffraction intensity maximum at angle θ = 50°.
de Broglie wavelength calculated: λ = 1.66 Å, matching Bragg's X-ray diffraction law: λ = 2 d sin ϕ = 1.65 Å.
cards.hint: Proved conclusively that electrons possess wave properties that undergo diffraction like X-rays.

cards.q: If the kinetic energy of a moving particle is increased by 16 times, how does its de Broglie wavelength change?
cards.a:
The wavelength becomes ONE-FOURTH (λ' = λ / 4)!
Since λ = h / √(2 m K) ⇒ λ ∝ 1 / √K. If K becomes 16 K, λ' = λ / √16 = λ / 4.
cards.hint: If momentum doubles (p' = 2p), wavelength halves (λ' = λ / 2).

cards.q: Number of photons emitted per second by a light source of power P and wavelength λ?
cards.a:
n = P / E_photon = P / (h ν) = (P · λ) / (h c).
Shortcut: E_photon (in eV) ≈ 12400 / λ (in Å) or 1240 / λ (in nm).
cards.hint: Useful shortcut for quick CET photon energy calculations without multiplying 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ by 3 × 10⁸.

cards.q: Photoelectric cell: Types and practical applications?
cards.a:
Types: Photoemissive cell, Photovoltaic cell, Photoconductive cell.
Applications: Burglar alarms, automated door openers, light meters in photography, sound reproduction in motion pictures, street light automated switches.
cards.hint: Converts light energy directly into electrical energy.

cards.q: If intensity of incident light on a photocell is doubled while frequency is kept constant, what happens to saturation current and stopping potential?
cards.a:
Saturation current DOUBLES (saturation current ∝ intensity).
Stopping potential remains COMPLETELY UNCHANGED (stopping potential depends strictly on frequency, NOT on intensity).
cards.hint: #1 MHT-CET trap! Doubling intensity increases number of emitted electrons, but not their individual energy.

cards.q: If frequency of incident light is doubled (with ν > ν₀), does the maximum kinetic energy also double?
cards.a:
NO! Maximum kinetic energy MORE THAN DOUBLES!
Since K_max = h ν - Φ₀: When ν becomes 2ν, K_max' = 2 h ν - Φ₀ = 2 (h ν - Φ₀) + Φ₀ = 2 K_max + Φ₀ > 2 K_max.
cards.hint: Classic entrance trap! Because work function Φ₀ is subtracted, K_max increases by more than a factor of 2.

cards.q: Wavelength λ of a photon vs de Broglie wavelength λ_e of an electron having same kinetic energy E?
cards.a:
Photon: λ_ph = h c / E.
Electron: λ_e = h / √(2 m E).
Ratio: λ_ph / λ_e = c √(2 m / E) ⇒ λ_ph ≫ λ_e for non-relativistic energies.
cards.hint: A photon always has a vastly longer wavelength than an electron with the same kinetic energy.

cards.q: Why is wave nature of matter not observable in everyday macroscopic objects (like a cricket ball)?
cards.a: Because macroscopic bodies have huge masses m, making their de Broglie wavelength λ = h / (m v) extraordinarily tiny (~10⁻³⁴ m), which is far smaller than any atomic dimensions and completely undetectable.
cards.hint: Diffraction effects require obstacle sizes comparable to wavelength λ.

cards.q: Photocurrent vs Anode Potential graph: Effect of varying intensity at constant frequency?
cards.a: Curves for different intensities originate from the SAME stopping potential -V₀ on negative voltage axis, but level off at DIFFERENT saturation currents proportional to intensity.
cards.hint: Confirms stopping potential is independent of light intensity.

cards.q: Photocurrent vs Anode Potential graph: Effect of varying frequency at constant intensity?
cards.a: Curves have DIFFERENT stopping potentials (-V₀₁ < -V₀₂ for ν₁ < ν₂), but attain the SAME saturation current.
cards.hint: Higher frequency requires a more negative stopping potential to halt electrons.

cards.q: Relation between threshold wavelength λ₀ and stopping potential V₀ when light of wavelength λ is incident?
cards.a: e V₀ = h c (1 / λ - 1 / λ₀) ⇒ V₀ = (h c / e) · [ (λ₀ - λ) / (λ · λ₀) ].
cards.hint: For photoemission to occur, incident wavelength λ must be strictly less than threshold wavelength λ₀ (λ ≤ λ₀).

cards.q: Effective mass of a photon of frequency ν?
cards.a: m = E / c² = h ν / c² = h / (c λ).
cards.hint: This is inertial mass in motion; rest mass is strictly zero.

cards.q: MHT-CET Trap: Light of wavelength λ falls on metal of work function Φ₀. If λ is halved, what is the new stopping potential?
cards.a:
e V₀' = 2 e V₀ + Φ₀ ⇒ V₀' = 2 V₀ + (Φ₀ / e).
New stopping potential is MORE than double the original stopping potential!
cards.hint: Since h c / (λ/2) = 2 (h c / λ) = 2 (e V₀ + Φ₀) = 2 e V₀ + 2 Φ₀ ⇒ e V₀' = 2 e V₀ + Φ₀.
